[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding Scope in Python (Local, Global, Nonlocal)"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Scope refers to the region of a program where a particular variable can be accessed. Understanding scope is crucial for writing clean, maintainable, and bug-free Python code. Python defines several types of scope: Local, Global, and Nonlocal. This tutorial will explain each of these scopes with examples."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Local Scope"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"A variable declared inside a function has local scope. This means it can only be accessed from within that function. Once the function finishes executing, the variable is no longer accessible."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"def my_function():
    x = 10  # x has local scope
    print("Value of x inside function:", x)

my_function()
# print(x)  # This would cause an error because x is not defined outside the function"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"In the example above, 'x' is only accessible within 'my_function()'. Attempting to access it outside the function will result in a 'NameError'."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Global Scope"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"A variable declared outside of any function or class has global scope. Global variables can be accessed from anywhere in the program, including inside functions."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"y = 20  # y has global scope

def another_function():
    print("Value of y inside function:", y)

another_function()
print("Value of y outside function:", y)"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Here, 'y' is defined outside any function, making it a global variable. Both 'another_function()' and the main part of the program can access 'y'."},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"If you want to modify a global variable from within a function, you need to use the 'global' keyword."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"z = 30

def modify_global():
    global z
    z = 40
    print("Value of z inside function:", z)

modify_global()
print("Value of z outside function:", z)"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Without the 'global' keyword, Python would create a new local variable named 'z' inside the function, leaving the global 'z' unchanged."},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Nonlocal Scope"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Nonlocal scope applies to nested functions. A nonlocal variable is neither local nor global, but it exists in the scope of an enclosing function. You use the 'nonlocal' keyword to indicate that a variable is nonlocal."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"def outer_function():
    x = 50

    def inner_function():
        nonlocal x
        x = 60
        print("Value of x inside inner function:", x)

    inner_function()
    print("Value of x inside outer function:", x)

outer_function()"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"In this example, 'x' is defined in 'outer_function()'. 'inner_function()' uses the 'nonlocal' keyword to modify 'x' in the enclosing scope. Without 'nonlocal', 'inner_function()' would create a new local variable named 'x'."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Local: Variables defined inside a function."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Global: Variables defined outside any function or class."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Nonlocal: Variables in the scope of an enclosing function (used in nested functions)."},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"Understanding these scope rules is essential for avoiding naming conflicts and ensuring that your code behaves as expected. Use the 'global' and 'nonlocal' keywords judiciously to maintain code clarity and prevent unintended side effects."}]
